# Load the Data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
install.packages("broom")
install.packages("knitr")
library(broom)
library(knitr)

movies <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2021/2021-03-09/movies.csv',
                          na = c("", "NA", "#N/A", "N/A"))
glimpse(movies)

# 1794 observations, 34 variables
```

# Section 1: Linear Regression
Research Question: Among these movies, how does domestic gross revenue change with budget? Is that pattern different for movies that pass vs. fail the Bechdel test?

    # Part A:
Budget_2013 has 0 missing values. Domgross_2013 has 18 missing values.

```{r}
# Summary of Budget variable
summary(movies$budget_2013)
# mean = 55,464,608, median = 36,995,786
# mean is very far from median, let's check the distribution in a histogram and boxplot
ggplot(movies, aes(x = budget_2013)) + geom_histogram() 
ggplot(movies, aes(x = budget_2013)) + geom_boxplot()
# The distribution is skewed heavily to the right, shown by both the histogram and the boxplot. The boxplot is showing lots and lots of outliers.
```

```{r}
# Summary of Domestic Gross Revenue variable
summary(movies$domgross_2013)
# mean = 9.517e+07, median = 5.599e+07
# again, mean far from median. Highest grossing/budgeted movies must be skewing the distribution quite a bit
ggplot(movies, aes(x = domgross_2013)) + geom_histogram() 
ggplot(movies, aes(x = domgross_2013)) + geom_boxplot()
# skewed to the right, lots of outliers 
```

```{r}
# Quick look at Bechdel Test variable
# 0 missing values
table(movies$binary) 
# 803 pass, 991 fail
table(movies$clean_test)
```

```{r}
# Try log-transforming the budget2013 and domgross2013 data to see if it's easier to see before we have to cut out super high outliers.
ggplot(movies, aes(x = log10(budget_2013))) + geom_histogram()
ggplot(movies, aes(x = log10(domgross_2013))) + geom_histogram()
# These look a little better, but I might get rid of some of the highest values along with the NAs, because they exhibit too much leverage anyway. 
```

Cleaning the Data: remove NAs and extreme values 

```{r}
# Removing NAs from domgross_2013
cleanrev_budget2013 <- movies %>% 
    filter(!is.na(domgross_2013), domgross_2013 < 5e+08) %>%
    filter(budget_2013 < 2.5e+08) %>%
    select(domgross_2013, budget_2013, binary)
summary(cleanrev_budget2013)
ggplot(cleanrev_budget2013, aes(x = domgross_2013)) + geom_boxplot()
ggplot(cleanrev_budget2013, aes(x = budget_2013)) + geom_boxplot()

# Looks a little better, going to proceed with this for now, looking at movies with a domestic gross revenue under 500 million dollars and budget under 250 million dollars. Hopefully this will result in the models fitting a little better with less extreme values that may cause it to overfit these really expensive values. And we want to get a general picture of the relationship between budget and revenue, not predicting whether a super high budget will produce a really high revenue.

```
